name: The Old Yew of Cremines (If millenaire)

location.address: Foret du Maljon, above Cremines, Bernese Jura

access: Free, public forest (Foret du Maljon). No path or signposts lead to it directly; the commune's own page says it stands hidden under rocks, off the walking paths, deliberately hard to find. Public land, not private, but expect a real search on foot.
transport: No public transport nearby; nearest station is Cremines on the Moutier-Solothurn line, then on foot up into the Maljon forest (steep, unmarked, roughly 45-60 min walk based on hiking-site descriptions; not verified by us step by step).
story:
Switzerland's oldest living tree has no path, no signpost and no bench, and the commune that owns it seems content to keep it that way. The yew in the Foret du Maljon above Cremines is put at around 1500 years old by the commune itself and by the Bern canton forestry division, which designated it an arbre monumental. Cremines calls it flatly le plus vieil arbre de Suisse.

Nobody has counted its rings. You cannot core a hollow, already damaged trunk without risking the thing you are trying to date, so the 1500 years is the settled estimate of the commune and the dendrological community rather than a measurement anyone took. The German tree register that also carries it lists 4.25 metres round and its condition as vital, and Swiss television filmed it as recently as 2023, which is the best evidence anyone has that it is still standing.

If the figure is even roughly right, this yew was young while the western Roman empire was coming apart, and it has been in the same wood through everything since, logged, replanted and walked over for fifteen centuries without anybody getting around to cutting it.

Finding it is the visit. It sits under rocks off the marked paths, and the commune's own page says plainly that it is hard to find. Take the coordinates, take an hour, and expect to search.

name: The Marthalen Oak

location.address: Abistwald forest, reached via the FC Ellikon/Marthalen football pitch, Marthalen

access: Free, in a public forest (Abistwald). The local museum's own visitor page says the path there crosses the FC Ellikon/Marthalen football pitch, and jokingly advises bringing a football along; no gate, ticket or restriction is mentioned.
transport: Marthalen railway station (Zurich-Schaffhausen line, roughly 25-30 min from Zurich HB) then on foot into the Abistwald, direction and distance not independently verified by us.
container: zurich (day trip, ~25-30 min by train, label as Marthalen)
story:
The walk to one of the oldest oaks in Switzerland crosses a football pitch, and the village museum that documents the tree advises bringing a ball.

The Ortsmuseum Marthalen puts the oak at over 360 years old, with a trunk 1.8 metres across, roughly 5.6 metres round, standing in the Abistwald north of the village. That museum is the only real source on it. Regional tourism pages repeat the same figures back, which is not the same thing as a second opinion, so read the age as the museum's estimate rather than a settled fact.

The forest around it does the corroborating. Marthalen's own timber inventory records an unusual concentration of very large stems here, over 112 centimetres in diameter at breast height and predominantly oak, a category with only a few dozen entries in the whole canton. This is not a lone survivor in a plantation. It is the biggest tree in a wood that has been growing big trees for a long time, in a village whose coat of arms is an oak.

Which oak it is remains open. Quercus robur and Quercus petraea both grow here and no source we found commits either way. If you can tell them apart by the acorn stalks and the leaf bases, you can settle this for us on the spot.

Marthalen is 25 to 30 minutes by direct train from Zurich.

name: The Plane Tree of the Ile de Peilz

location.address: Viewed from the Quai Grand Rive shoreline, Villeneuve, looking out to the Ile de Peilz islet in Lake Geneva

access: Free, view-only. Both sources are explicit that the islet itself cannot be visited (2tout2rien.fr: "L'ilot ne se visite pas"; Wikipedia: boat approach risks running aground and is not recommended). It is viewed from the public lakefront quays of Villeneuve (Quai Grand Rive is named as the classic viewpoint) or from a boat on the lake, best at sunrise or sunset when the tree silhouettes.
transport: Villeneuve VD railway station, then a short walk along the lakefront quay.
story:
Lake Geneva has exactly one natural island, it is roughly the size of a large living room, and the single tree standing on it is one you are not allowed to reach.

The Ile de Peilz is a rock off Villeneuve that local people built up with earth, by tradition in 1797. Three plane trees went in in 1851. By 1970 one plane and an ailing horse chestnut were left; the chestnut has since died, and the plane now stands alone at roughly 175 years old, filling its entire island. A certified arborist assessed it in 2023 and found it generally healthy, with some decay present but nothing that stops it working.

It was famous before anyone photographed it. Byron wrote the islet into The Prisoner of Chillon in 1816, before the trees existed. Hans Christian Andersen put it in The Ice-Maiden in 1861, when they were ten years old. Since around 2021 it has become one of the most photographed objects on the lake.

You look rather than visit. Both sources are explicit that the islet cannot be landed on and that a boat risks running aground trying. The view is from the public quays at Villeneuve, and our pin marks that shoreline rather than the tree. Go at either end of the day, when the plane turns to a silhouette against open water.

name: The Linden of Morat
age_estimate: planted 1984, a direct cutting of a tree first recorded in the 15th century

location.address: Place de l'Hotel-de-Ville, next to the Fontaine Saint-Georges, Bourg quarter, Fribourg

access: Free, a public town square in the historic Bourg quarter of Fribourg.
transport: Fribourg/Freiburg railway station, then roughly a 15-20 minute walk down into the Bourg quarter (not independently timed by us).
story:
In 1476 a messenger is said to have run from the battlefield at Morat to Fribourg waving a linden branch cut on the field, collapsed in the Bourg quarter, and the branch took root where he fell. That is the legend. The tree on the Place de l'Hotel-de-Ville today is a cutting of the tree the legend was told about, planted in 1984, and it is about forty years old.

The original tilleul de Morat is recorded from the fifteenth century and stood in the Bourg for five hundred years. In 1983 a vehicle hit it and it had to be taken down. The University of Fribourg's botanical garden had kept a cutting, and that cutting went into the ground the following year beside the Fontaine Saint-Georges, where it still stands.

So this is a young tree at a very old address, which is both the honest description and the interesting one. Fribourg has not let go of the story: there has been a television segment, a museum exhibition devoted to the linden, and for the battle's 550th anniversary in 2026 a second cutting is being planted about a hundred metres away on the Rue des Alpes.

The square is public and free. The run is a legend, the felling is documented, and the tree in front of you is genetically the same plant as the one that fell.

best_time.label: late June into July, when the lime flowers and the square smells of them

name: The Linden of Linn
access: Free, public. Directly at the 'Boezberg, Linn' bus stop, marking the village entrance; also reachable on a 20-minute waymarked walk from Boezberg-Neustalden station. Aargau Tourismus's own page (updated 2026-08-04) notes it is 'very popular and well-visited', suggesting a weekday or early Sunday visit for a quieter one.
transport: From Zurich: train to Brugg, then onward bus/local transport toward Boezberg/Linn; total journey likely 45-60 minutes each way (not independently timed step by step by us; this is a longer trip than the classic 30-minute day-trip case and should be labelled honestly as such).
container: zurich (day trip, borderline distance ~32km / real journey likely 45-60 min via Brugg, label honestly as Linn/Boezberg; flagging for a judgement call rather than asserting confidently)
story:
Local legend says that if this linden's shadow ever stops reaching Habsburg Castle, the world ends. The tree is eleven metres round, twenty-five metres tall and roughly 800 years old, which by the canton's own reckoning makes it the mightiest tree in Aargau and would make it a sapling around the time Rudolf von Habsburg, founder of the dynasty the castle is named for, was born.

A second legend is more popular and less durable: that survivors of the plague planted it, in the sixteenth or seventeenth century. The tree's own dating rules that out by several hundred years. Both stories are worth knowing, only one of them can be true, and it is the tree that settles the argument.

Eleven metres of circumference is enormous even for a large-leaved lime, a species that fuses, splits and re-roots itself into fluted multi-stemmed trunks as it ages. What you walk up to is less a trunk than a small ruined building with leaves on top.

It stands at the entrance to Linn village, directly at the bus stop, and Aargau's tourist board calls it very popular, which is a polite warning about Sunday afternoons. From Zurich this is a real trip rather than a stroll: train to Brugg, then a local connection onward, 45 to 60 minutes each way.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and all eleven metres of trunk stand exposed
